name: Kɔlɛ / Kole

catalog_quote: 2.1.4 Tones The kɔlɛ language makes use of four level tones. These tones are H (high), L (low), LH (low-high rising tone), HL (high-low falling tone). Examples kpérí "death" / èkpà "bag" / ŋgbâ "dog" / yětà "reply" [p. 24] The following tonal systems are found in kɔlɛ a) monosyllabic kɔ́ "snail", mbɔ̀ "honey" b) disyllabic dìbé "breast", ŋgɔ́lì "belt", mbɔ́à "village", ngìrà "lion" c) trisyllabic kárárá "corn", mótùtù "smoke", mùkèyé "egg", mòkókó "sugercane", ìréndè "knife"
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (130 pp., Acrobat Capture text) and rendered p. 29 (printed p. 23) to an image. The quote is there verbatim under heading '2.1.4 Tones': 'The kɔlɛ language makes use of four level tones. These tones are H (high), L (low), LH (low-high rising tone), HL (high-low falling tone).' followed by examples kpérí 'death', èkpà 'bag', ŋgbâ 'dog', yětà 'reply' (not mentioned in the report; immaterial). The text renders kɔlɛ as 'kale' and 'tones' as 'torLes', as the compiler noted. Printed p. 24 (PDF 30) gives the mono-/di-/trisyllabic tone-pattern nouns; p. 25 begins Chapter III Noun Class System, so the phonology chapter is exactly pp. 16-24 as stated. I read the whole of Chapter II (PDF 22-30)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress: the only accessible description presents Kɔlɛ as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (LH, HL) contrasting on nouns, and never mentions word stress, accent or prominence. Nothing can be said about where stress falls; the source is silent on it rather than denying it.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the section is a two-page résumé of the tonal system, explicitly based on Ewota 1973 (p. 16).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: citation forms of nouns (mono-, di- and trisyllabic) in isolation, e.g. kɔ́ 'snail', mbɔ̀ 'honey', dìbé 'breast', mbɔ́à 'village', kárárá 'corn', mɔ̀kɔ́kɔ́ 'sugarcane', ìréndè 'knife' (p. 24). Vowel length is said to be non-phonemic (p. 16); syllable structure (C)V(C), predominantly open CV (pp. 21-22). Noun-class prefixes are stated to be always low-toned ('The tone for the noun prefixes are always low', concord chapter).
new_statements.identity_note: Asobo 1989 describes the Kɔlɛ (Kole) spoken in the six fishing settlements around Bamusso (Bekanje, Ubenikang, Betika, Njangasa, Bekumu, Yenda, Bamusso), Ndian division, SW Cameroon, ~400 speakers in 1989; identified by the author with ALCAM no. 625 'bakole' and with Guthrie A.20 (Duala-Limbe group). This is Glottolog bako1250 / ISO kme itself, not a differently named variety. Note that English Wikipedia redirects 'Bakole language' to Kpwe (Mokpwe, bri, mokp1239), calling Kole mutually intelligible with Kpwe; Glottolog and ISO keep it a separate language, and Asobo's data were collected from Kole speakers. Ebobissé 2014 treats Kole (KOL) as one of the Sawabantu lects.

sources.citation: English Wikipedia, 'Kpwe language' (to which 'Bakole language' redirects), citing Atindogbé 2013, A grammatical sketch of Mòkpè (Bakweri), African Study Monographs Suppl. 45: 5-163.
sources.note: Treats Kole as mutually intelligible with Kpwe; gives a five-tone system for Kpwe (high, downstepped high, low, rising, falling) and says nothing about stress or about Kole specifically. Not a Bakole source.

sources.citation: Ebobissé, Carl. 1989. Dialectométrie lexicale des parlers Sawabantu. Journal of West African Languages 19(2): 57-66.
sources.note: Lexicostatistic classification of the Sawabantu lects including Kole; unlikely to discuss stress but is the earliest modern published treatment that places Kole; useful for the identity note.
Segment inventory only, derived from Asobo 1989; no prosodic statement. Confirms Asobo 1989 is the only phonological source in the database for this language.

sources.note: The only descriptive items for Bakole are Ewota 1973 (phonology), Asobo 1989 (grammar sketch) and Ebobissé 2014 (comparative overview/wordlist); the rest are sociolinguistic/endangerment surveys (Connell 2007, Sommer 1992, Moseley 2010) and Ardener 1956 (ethnographic overview). The kole1239 list adds only Isubu/Wovea material (Mokake 2021 reference grammar of Isubu, Sirih-Nagang 2020, Merrick 1854, Saker 1852) which concerns the sister language szv, not Bakole.
